title: CRDTs in Depth
summary: Conflict Resolution's one-slide mention of CRDTs, expanded into the actual data types and the guarantee that makes them mergeable without coordination.

slides.markdown:
[Conflict resolution](conflict-resolution) introduced CRDTs as one option among several. This topic goes deeper: what specific guarantee makes a CRDT mergeable without coordination, the two families of CRDTs (state-based and operation-based), the actual data types you'd reach for, and where the pattern shows up in real products.

The short version: a CRDT is a data type engineered so that "merge" has exactly one correct, unambiguous answer — no matter how the two replicas got out of sync.

slides.sectionTitle: The guarantee CRDTs make: any two replicas' states merge into the same result, regardless of order
slides.markdown:
The formal name for what a CRDT guarantees is **strong eventual consistency**: any two replicas that have seen the same set of updates — in any order, with any duplicates — will merge to the exact same state. This is a much stronger claim than plain eventual consistency, which only promises convergence *eventually*, with no guarantee about how or whether every possible ordering agrees.

The mathematical property behind this is that a CRDT's merge operation is **commutative** (order doesn't matter), **associative** (grouping doesn't matter), and **idempotent** (applying the same update twice doesn't change the result twice). Any data type with a merge function satisfying those three properties is a CRDT by definition.

That's why CRDTs don't need coordination, locking, or consensus to merge safely — the math guarantees there's only ever one right answer.

slides.sectionTitle: State-based (CvRDT) vs operation-based (CmRDT) CRDTs: sending state vs sending operations
slides.markdown:
CRDTs split into two families based on what replicas actually send each other.

| | State-based (CvRDT) | Operation-based (CmRDT) |
|---|---|---|
| What's sent between replicas | The entire current state | Just the individual operation (e.g. "increment by 1") |
| Merge happens by | Combining two full states with a merge function | Applying the operation directly, assuming it's delivered at least once |
| Network cost | Higher — full state grows with data size | Lower — small messages, but needs reliable, order-tolerant delivery |
| Tolerates duplicate delivery | Yes, inherently (merge is idempotent) | Only if operations are also designed to be idempotent |

**How to decide:** CvRDTs are simpler to reason about and forgive an unreliable network (resend the whole state, no harm done); CmRDTs are cheaper on the wire but need more care in the messaging layer to avoid double-applying an operation.

slides.markdown:
![Two replicas diverging with concurrent updates and merging back to the same state](assets/crdt-merge.svg)

The picture is the whole point of a CRDT: divergence during the network partition is expected and harmless, because the merge step is guaranteed to bring both replicas back to the *same* combined state — not an approximation, the same state, bit for bit.

slides.sectionTitle: Common CRDTs: G-Counter/PN-Counter, OR-Set, and LWW-Register
slides.markdown:
A handful of CRDTs cover most practical needs. A **G-Counter** (grow-only counter) tracks a per-replica increment count and merges by taking the max of each replica's count, then summing — it can only go up. A **PN-Counter** (positive-negative counter) adds a second G-Counter for decrements, so the visible value is `increments - decrements`, supporting both directions.

An **OR-Set** (observed-remove set) lets elements be added and removed concurrently without the classic "add-wins or remove-wins" ambiguity, by tagging each add with a unique identifier so a later remove only removes the adds it actually observed.

An **LWW-Register** holds a single value resolved by timestamp on merge — effectively last-write-wins packaged as a formal CRDT, useful when you specifically want that trade-off and want it to compose cleanly with other CRDTs.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: implementing a PN-Counter that merges correctly under concurrent increments and decrements
Where CRDTs actually get used: collaborative editors, offline-first mobile apps, shopping carts
slides.markdown:
**Collaborative editors** (the kind that let two people edit the same document simultaneously and reconcile changes without a server round-trip) frequently use text-specific CRDTs to merge concurrent edits deterministically — the exact scenario a design-collaborative-editor question is probing.

**Offline-first mobile apps** — note-taking, to-do lists — use CRDTs so a device can keep working fully offline and merge cleanly once it reconnects, with no server needed to arbitrate at merge time.

**Shopping carts**, Dynamo's original motivating example, map naturally onto an OR-Set: items added on two devices both survive the merge.

The common thread: CRDTs fit whenever "work offline, merge automatically, no coordinator required" is a real product requirement, not just a nice-to-have.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: CRDTs vs operational transformation (OT) for collaborative editing
slides.markdown:
| | CRDTs | Operational Transformation (OT) |
|---|---|---|
| Coordination needed | None — merge is commutative by construction | Usually needs a central server to transform and order operations |
| Works fully offline/peer-to-peer | Yes, naturally | Harder — traditional OT assumes a server broker |
| Complexity | Complexity lives in designing the right CRDT for text | Complexity lives in the transformation functions themselves |
| Real-world use | Automerge, Yjs, Riak's data types | Google Docs' original architecture |

**How to decide:** pick CRDTs when you need true peer-to-peer or offline-first editing with no central server; OT remains viable when you already have a central server in the loop and want its long, battle-tested track record (Google Docs).

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reaching for a CRDT for data where "merge both" is actually the wrong business answer
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "CRDTs solve conflicts automatically, so let's use one for every piece of shared state."

**Why it's wrong:** a CRDT's merge rule is fixed by the data type's math, not by what's actually correct for the business. An OR-Set union works great for a shopping cart (both additions should survive) but is actively wrong for, say, a seat reservation — merging two concurrent "reserve seat 12A" operations from different users by keeping both isn't a resolved conflict, it's a double-booking.

**Correct model:** ask what the correct outcome of a concurrent conflict actually is before picking a CRDT. If the true answer requires picking exactly one winner or applying business rules (checking inventory, confirming only one reservation), a CRDT's automatic "merge both" isn't a shortcut — it's the wrong answer wearing a mathematically elegant disguise.
